passages.t: Heaven is God's throne, and he looks to the humble
passages.happening:
‘This is what the LORD says’ (verse 1). Heaven is his throne and earth his footstool. What house could anyone build for him, or where could he rest (verse 1)? His hand made all these things (verse 2). And this is the one he esteems: ‘he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word’ (verse 2).

Worship offered by people who choose their own way is as bad as the worst rites. ‘Whoever slaughters an ox is like one who slays a man; whoever sacrifices a lamb is like one who breaks a dog’s neck’ (verse 3). They have chosen their own ways (verse 3). So God will choose their punishment, ‘because I called and no one answered, I spoke and no one listened’ (verse 4).

Those who tremble at his word are to hear him. Their own brothers who hate them and shut them out because of God's name mock them, but those brothers will be put to shame (verse 5). There is an uproar from the city, a voice from the temple: the LORD repaying his enemies (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The book ends much as it began. Chapter 1 called heaven and earth as witnesses, rejected sacrifices from people with bloody hands, and set rebels against the faithful. Chapter 66 does the same, but everything has grown: the small remnant has become a nation, and the heavens and earth are new.

The question about a house for God fits a time when the temple was being rebuilt or newly finished, about 515 BC, and many scholars place the chapter there. Some read verse 1 as opposing the rebuilding. Most see it as correcting a wrong trust in the building, since verses 6 and 20 still speak of God's voice from the temple and offerings brought there. Those who take the whole book as Isaiah's read it as prophecy for that community.

Verse 3 sets proper sacrifices beside horrors: an ox beside murder, a lamb beside breaking a dog's neck, though dogs were unclean and never offered. Worship from people who have chosen their own ways offends God as much as the worst rites.

The word for tremble, chared, marks the true people of God. Ezra uses it for those who trembled at God's commands. Verse 5 shows division inside the people of God itself, brothers shutting out the faithful.
passages.later: Stephen quotes verses 1 and 2 before the council: ‘Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool’ (Acts 7:49). Ezra describes ‘everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel’ (Ezra 9:4).
passages.asks: God says he looks to the one who trembles at his word. Ask how you take God's word: as information, or with something like trembling. And ask whether you trust a building, a ritual or a habit more than the God who made heaven.

passages.t: Zion gives birth, and God comforts like a mother
passages.happening:
Before Zion was in labor, she gave birth; before the pain came, she delivered a son (verse 7). ‘Who has heard of such as this? Who has seen such things? Can a country be born in a day or a nation be delivered in an instant?’ (verse 8). As soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children (verse 8). God will not bring a child to the moment of birth and not deliver it (verse 9).

‘Be glad for Jerusalem and rejoice over her, all who love her’ (verse 10). All who mourned over her will nurse at her comforting breast and be satisfied (verse 11). God will extend peace to her like a river, and the wealth of nations like a flowing stream. Her children will be carried on her arm and bounced on her knees (verse 12).

Then God says what he will be. ‘As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you, and you will be consoled over Jerusalem’ (verse 13). They will see it and rejoice and flourish like grass (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The birth picture comes from ordinary family life. Mothers nursed their children for years, carried them on the hip and played with them on their knees. The poem first compares Zion to such a mother. Then God compares himself to one.

A country born in a day was the opposite of what the returned exiles knew. They lived through slow, small, painful rebuilding. The poem promises that what seemed impossible will happen suddenly, without the long labor.

The word comfort, nacham, appears three times in verse 13. The second half of Isaiah opened with Comfort, comfort (40:1). Here, near the end, the promise of comfort is kept to the last page, and the one who comforts is God himself, like a mother.
passages.later: The second half of Isaiah began with this word: ‘Comfort, comfort My people,’ says your God (Isaiah 40:1). A psalm uses the same picture: ‘like a weaned child with his mother’ (Psalm 131:2).
passages.asks: God says he will comfort his people as a mother comforts her son. Ask what it means to you that God describes himself this way. And ask who in your life needs that kind of comfort, and whether you could give some of it.

passages.t: Fire, the nations gathered, and the last word
passages.happening:
‘For behold, the LORD will come with fire’ (verse 15), with chariots like a whirlwind. By fire and sword he will judge all flesh (verse 16). Those who purify themselves for the rites in the groves and eat swine and rats will perish together (verse 17).

God knows their deeds and thoughts, and he is coming ‘to gather all nations and tongues, and they will come and see My glory’ (verse 18). He will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Put and Lud, to Tubal and Javan and the far islands that have not heard of his fame, and they will proclaim his glory among the nations (verse 19). They will bring all Zion's brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD, on horses and chariots, mules and camels (verse 20). God will even choose some of them as priests and Levites (verse 21).

As the new heavens and new earth will endure, so will their descendants and their name (verse 22). From one New Moon to another and one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before the LORD (verse 23). As they go out, they will see the corpses of those who rebelled, whose worm will not die and whose fire will not be quenched (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Verse 19 names distant peoples at the edges of the known world. Tarshish was a far western port, often linked with southern Spain. Put was in Africa, probably near Libya; the Hebrew text reads Pul, and the BSB follows the Greek reading Put. Lud is usually taken as Lydia in western Asia Minor, though some place it in Africa. Tubal was in eastern Asia Minor, and Javan is the Hebrew name for the Greeks. Survivors are sent to them as messengers, and some of the nations' people become priests.

The New Moon and the Sabbath were Israel's regular times of worship. The prophet pictures all mankind keeping that rhythm before God.

The corpses of verse 24 recall the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place of burning linked with child sacrifice, and later, under the name Gehenna, with final judgment. In the synagogue, verse 23 is repeated after verse 24 when Isaiah is read, so that the reading does not end on the corpses.
passages.later: Jesus quotes verse 24 when he warns about Gehenna, where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched’ (Mark 9:48). The book began with a call to the same witnesses: ‘Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth’ (Isaiah 1:2), and the rebels of Jeremiah 7 had burned their children in the same valley.
passages.hard:
Why does such a hopeful book end with corpses and an undying worm?

Many readers find the last verse jarring, and Jewish practice answers by repeating verse 23 after it. Still, the ending is deliberate. Isaiah has spoken from the first chapter of two ways, trust in God or rebellion, and the book will not pretend the choice does not matter. The worshipers go out and see what rebellion finally comes to: death outside the city. The picture recalls the Valley of Hinnom, where Judah had burned children to other gods, so the judgment falls on the very place of Judah's worst sin.

Christians have drawn on this verse, as Jesus did, in teaching about final judgment, and they differ on its exact meaning. Traditional teaching reads it as eternal, conscious punishment. Others hold that the wicked are finally destroyed, the undying worm and fire describing a destruction that cannot be reversed. A smaller number hope for the eventual restoration of all. The main traditions agree that the verse is a warning given while there is still time to turn, and that the God who ends the book with judgment is the same God who has held out his hands all day long.
passages.asks: The book's last scene sets worshipers from every nation beside the end of rebellion. Ask which of the two ways your life is walking. And ask what it would mean for you to be one of the survivors sent to tell the far islands about God's glory.
